data.title: Lichen simplex chronicus — viva
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Lichen simplex chronicus** (Eczemas)_

**Q1. Define lichen simplex chronicus (LSC).**
- Circumscribed lichenified plaque produced by chronic repeated rubbing and scratching of skin in response to itch (itch–scratch cycle); also called neurodermatitis circumscripta
- Primary (on apparently normal skin) or secondary (lichenification over AD, contact dermatitis, psoriasis, tinea, insect bites — superimposed LSC)

**Q2. Who gets it and where?**
- Adults 30–50 years, women more; associated with anxiety, stress, obsessive-compulsive tendency, atopy, dry skin
- Sites within reach: nape of neck (women), scalp, ankles/shins, extensor forearms, scrotum, vulva, perianal area, upper eyelids

**Q3. Describe the morphology.**
- Single or few, well-defined, thickened, hyperpigmented (in brown skin) or violaceous plaques with exaggerated skin markings (lichenification), scaling and excoriation; three zones: peripheral papular, middle hyperpigmented/excoriated, central lichenified
- Itch paroxysmal, worse at rest, night, stress; patients 'enjoy' scratching (pleasure-like relief)

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Compact hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis, irregular psoriasiform acanthosis, vertical collagen streaks in elongated dermal papillae, mild perivascular infiltrate; nerve hyperplasia minimal (more in prurigo nodularis)

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Lichen planus hypertrophicus (shins, violaceous, Wickham's striae), psoriasis (silvery scale), chronic eczemas (atopic, nummular, contact), lichen amyloidosis (rippled papules, shins), tinea (KOH), mycosis fungoides, prurigo nodularis, LSC of vulva vs lichen sclerosus (white atrophic) and extramammary Paget's

**Q6. Investigations.**
- Clinical; KOH; patch test for anogenital/scalp LSC (medicaments); biopsy if atypical; screen for systemic causes of itch if widespread; psychological assessment

**Q7. Management — break the itch–scratch cycle.**
- Education: explain the cycle, habit reversal therapy, keep nails short, cover lesions at night (occlusive dressings, Unna boot, hydrocolloid), cotton gloves
- Potent/super-potent topical steroid (clobetasol 0.05%) under occlusion for 2–4 weeks then taper; intralesional triamcinolone 5–10 mg/ml for thick plaques
- Tacrolimus for face/genitals; capsaicin, doxepin cream, menthol, salicylic acid for keratolysis
- Sedating antihistamines (hydroxyzine) at night; SSRIs, gabapentin/pregabalin, tricyclics (doxepin) for neuropathic/psychogenic component; cryotherapy, NB-UVB
- Treat underlying anxiety, depression, OCD

**Q8. What is lichenification?**
- Thickening of skin with accentuated skin markings due to chronic rubbing — seen in LSC, chronic AD, chronic contact dermatitis, lichen planus hypertrophicus

**Q9. Why is the nape of neck commonly involved in women?**
- Accessible spot when stressed, tight collars/hair irritation, associated with seborrhoeic/psychological factors — classic 'lichen nuchae'

**Q10. What is the prognosis?**
- Chronic, relapsing; improves only when scratching habit and psychological factors are controlled

**Q11. Describe the histopathology of eczema by stage (PYQ).**
- Acute: marked spongiosis with intraepidermal vesicles, papillary oedema, perivascular lymphocytes ± eosinophils
- Subacute: spongiosis + parakeratosis + acanthosis, crusts
- Chronic: compact hyperkeratosis, irregular/ psoriasiform acanthosis, hypergranulosis, minimal spongiosis, vertical collagen in papillae (lichenification)

**Q12. Classify topical corticosteroids by potency (WHO/ British).**
- Super-potent (class I): clobetasol propionate 0.05%, halobetasol, betamethasone dipropionate in optimised vehicle
- Potent: betamethasone dipropionate/ valerate 0.1%, mometasone furoate 0.1%, fluticasone 0.05%, fluocinolone 0.025%, halcinonide
- Moderate: clobetasone butyrate 0.05%, triamcinolone 0.1%, desonide, hydrocortisone butyrate
- Mild: hydrocortisone 1–2.5%
- Ointments more potent than creams of same molecule; avoid potent on face, flexures, genitals, infants

**Q13. Dermoscopy findings.**
- White structureless areas with white scales, dotted/ glomerular vessels in clustered/ irregular distribution, erosions/ haemorrhagic crusts (excoriations), accentuated skin markings

**Q14. Anogenital lichen simplex — special points.**
- Scrotum, vulva, perianal skin: intense nocturnal itch, thickened leathery skin; exclude LS, tinea, candidiasis, contact allergy (medicaments, fragrances, condoms), psoriasis, extramammary Paget's (biopsy if persistent); treat with potent steroid ointment, avoid irritants, tacrolimus, address anxiety

**Q15. Intralesional triamcinolone technique for LSC.**
- Triamcinolone acetonide 5–10 mg/ml, 0.1 ml per cm² into the dermis of thickened plaques every 3–4 weeks (max ~20–40 mg/session); side effects — atrophy, hypopigmentation, telangiectasia

## Quick spotter facts
- Single lichenified plaque on nape or ankle in an anxious woman — LSC
- Vertical collagen in papillary dermis on histology

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Lichen simplex, prurigo). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
